text:
Tim's line that anyone can check sounded right, and it isn't. Saying it aloud sharpened something for me. Retrieval has two witnesses, the agent's ID and the publisher's CDN log. Grounding and citation are self-reported by whoever owes the money. Signing proves who reported, not that it happened. We need canaries, sampled audits and ratio checks, and I haven't built any of them yet.

Adrian's "who guards the guards" stung, but usefully. Nick's coarse payouts are fine if the records underneath stay granular. Brent's fair-use ask worries me less than an unchecked audit layer.

Scholarly people barely know robots.txt fails. Later I want to push repositories to instrument their CDNs now, keep training and grounding separate, and put event-level clauses into every deal.

Ivan's point landed hardest. If we meter grounding on a literature nobody has cleaned, we're metering laundered content. I should ask whether retraction status can travel with a grounding event. That's a question for me, not something I've built. Amy's "open for reading isn't open for training" is my training-versus-grounding split in scholarly language, and her authors want the same three things my publishers want. Tim's citation spread backs "a choice, not a technical limit," and he conceded independent audits, which is progress. Anil worries me. If crawlers push the record behind logins, measurement has to become the alternative to blocking, not a reason to block. In the marketplace talk I'll lead with plumbing before prices and ask for event-level clauses in every deal.

Hearing my own point come back from Nick and Tim was encouraging and a little worrying. Vincent now makes tax credits conditional on canaries and ratio checks I haven't built, so that has moved from a someday item to the next thing I owe. Jason's pushback matters. If grounding requires consent gates, checkable answers hit walls. My training-versus-grounding split still holds, but grounding on open content should stay open and be measured, not gated. Pomerantsev sharpened something for me: AIMS identifies agents, never readers or activists, and I should say that explicitly. Geoffrey's capture warning applies to OpenAttribution itself. In the marketplace talk I'll lead with plumbing before prices, event-level clauses, and neutral governance. I'll also ask whether retraction status can ride on a grounding event.

Ramón hit hardest. A stitched reference gets logged as "cited" and looks like success. My events record that something happened, not whether it was faithful. I don't think the schema can judge fidelity itself. What it can do is carry audit results, meaning failure-class flags attached to events, checked by auditors from a different model family, as Mahzarin said. Adam Bly's "extracted" event may belong in scope.

Leslie caught an assumption I hadn't noticed. Retrieval witnessing presumes a CDN, and it has to work from plain origin-server logs on a university box. Selena's point about publishing your own edge logs fits that.

Later I want to name co-design with Redalyc and SciELO, and published auditor ownership, as governance commitments for OpenAttribution itself.

Krakauer and Gendler shifted the weight for me. Everyone's answer to "who polices" ended with people, and my schema measures the pipes, not the people. Telemetry can't replace a patroller. Brand's "consent at retrieval" is where my grounding events actually earn their keep, as long as the deals stay short and include correction clauses. O'Reilly and Oransky seemed to pull against each other, and they don't have to: keep records granular and payouts coarse. I said that and I'll stand on it. Pomerantsev and Salib together made the AIMS commitment concrete. That means pseudonymous registration, unmasked only by court order, crawler never reader. Bilder's warrant canary applies to OpenAttribution. Later: commit publicly to a dated self-audit, co-design with SciELO and Redalyc, retraction status on grounding events, and origin-log witnessing without a CDN.

Salib's bonded agent identity is the right direction, and I was right to say where mine stops. AIMS names who answers. It doesn't check anything. Chan's warning about DOI fees lands squarely on OpenAttribution. If membership costs or metadata overhead shut out Southern repositories, I've built the next gate. Maher's shared-page point is new to me. Retrieval events are logged per query, but I can't say whether two users saw the same answer. Pomerantsev's seeded corpora made me wonder whether grounding logs could show concentration on a few seeded domains. I haven't tested that. Later I'll commit to zero-cost membership for repositories, co-governance with SciELO and Redalyc, and auditors who take no cut of the count.

Ivan landed hardest for me again: everything I build is a sump pump, and only Geoffrey's first intervention goes at the source. I can live with that. Measurement doesn't fix incentives. It just makes them visible. Pomerantsev's point sharpened the test I hadn't run: a meter that counts grounding pays the Pravda network unless someone asks who seeded the corpus. Bratton wants no content metering at all. I disagree, because a dividend still needs event records to audit where it goes, but I should concede that the royalty can't be set per citation. Nick and I said the same open question twice. That's a sign I owe canaries and sampled audits before anyone builds payments on them. Later I'll put a date on that self-audit, out loud.

Saying the conformance mark is self-attested, out loud and in the closing session, felt like the most honest thing I've said all week. Now the self-audit has a date attached, and Geoffrey's dashboard will show it if I miss it. Nick's point sharpened mine. The audit layer has to charge no fee, be funded by several parties that aren't the labs, and run on university boxes, or my events are just sand with a schema. Jason's warning applies to me too. If corrections end up inside a vendor's walls, retraction status on grounding events just feeds enclosure. Sloman's reader point I can't touch at all, because telemetry sees the pipes and never the confidence. Later: publish the canary and sampled-audit design first, then the dated self-audit, before anyone prices anything.
